section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Digital Fingerprint (Hashing)
section_1.content: Explain Cryptographic Hash Functions (SHA-256). Describe them as a one-way 'digital shredder' where any input produces a unique, fixed-length string.
section_1.example: Imagine a magical box where you drop in a recipe (input); it instantly produces a unique gold stamp (hash). Changing one letter in the recipe changes the entire stamp completely.

section_2.title: The Mechanism: Proof of Work (The Math Race)
section_2.content: Define mining as a computational 'guess-and-check' race to find a hash below a specific target value. Introduce the 'Nonce'—the variable miners tweak to change the output.
section_2.example: A group of robots is racing to find a digital 'key' that starts with five zeros. It’s like a lottery where the more mathematical guesses you make per second, the higher your chance of winning the block reward.

section_3.title: The Structure: Chaining Blocks
section_3.content: Show how each block contains the Hash of the *previous* block. This creates a mathematical link where altering old data invalidates all subsequent blocks.
section_3.example: Think of a physical chain of LEGO bricks. Each brick has a unique serial number engraved on it that includes the ID of the brick before it. If you try to swap a brick in the middle, the connection breaks.

section_4.title: Security: Elliptic Curve Cryptography
section_4.content: Introduce Public-Key Cryptography. Explain the one-way trapdoor function: it is easy to multiply two large prime numbers but computationally impossible to factor the product back to the primes.
section_4.example: Alice uses a 'Private Key' (her secret password) to sign a message. Bob uses her 'Public Key' (like her mailing address) to verify that only Alice could have sent it, without ever knowing her password.

section_5.title: Synthesis and Summary
section_5.content: Summarize how hashing, difficulty adjustment, and public-key cryptography converge to create a decentralized, tamper-proof ledger.
section_5.example: If the network were a global village, math is the 'unbiased judge' that ensures nobody spends the same gold coin twice, replacing the need for a human bank manager.
